blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — OTC pseudoephedrine hypertension precaution
stem: A client with hypertension asks whether it is safe to self-treat nasal congestion with pseudoephedrine. What should the nurse advise?

options.A: Ask a doctor before using pseudoephedrine because the OTC label lists high blood pressure as a condition requiring medical advice.
options.B: Use pseudoephedrine at the labeled dose without consultation as long as prescribed antihypertensive medication is taken that day.
options.C: Take one-half of the labeled pseudoephedrine dose without consultation because dose reduction removes the blood-pressure precaution.
options.D: Choose an extended-release pseudoephedrine product without consultation because slower absorption avoids the hypertension warning.

rationale: Current OTC pseudoephedrine Drug Facts labeling instructs consumers to ask a doctor before use if they have high blood pressure. Therefore A is the appropriate teaching. Taking antihypertensive medication, reducing the pseudoephedrine dose, or choosing an extended-release formulation does not remove the label's requirement for medical advice before use in a person with hypertension.
educational_objective: Teach clients with hypertension to seek medical advice before using OTC pseudoephedrine because high blood pressure is specifically listed under the label's 'Ask a doctor before use' warnings.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA OTC labeling
source_document_title: Pseudoephedrine Hydrochloride Extended-Release Tablets — Drug Facts
source_version_date: DailyMed Drug Facts updated February 3, 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Warnings — Ask a doctor before use if you have: heart disease; high blood pressure; thyroid disease; diabetes; trouble urinating due to an enlarged prostate gland.
source_claim_supported: The OTC pseudoephedrine label directs people with high blood pressure to ask a doctor before use.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: educate client about medications; review pertinent data prior to medication administration; administer medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as plausible self-treatment decisions of nearly identical length.
Retained one exact OTC label-supported recommendation and removed the original weak distractors.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A is the only choice that follows the current OTC label. The options are length-matched and all address the same decision construct, excluding cueing and a second defensible answer.
